drills.los_text: discuss financial risks associated with the portfolio strategy of an institutional investor
drills.reading_name: Case Study in Portfolio Management: Institutional (SWF)

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund was established to grow the proceeds of a large deposit of non-renewable rare earth metals and is classified as a savings fund. The fund is most likely intended to:

options.A: fund the government's annual operating budget.
options.B: distribute cash to citizens each year.
options.C: share resource wealth across generations.

rationales.A: Funding the annual operating budget is the mandate of a stabilization or fiscal fund, not a savings fund. A stabilization fund holds short-duration, liquid assets so that it can smooth government revenue from one year to the next, and its asset allocation is built around that call on the money. A savings fund faces no such call and therefore invests on an intergenerational horizon.
rationales.B: Immediate annual cash distributions to citizens describe a different fund type again. A savings fund retains and compounds the capital rather than paying it out, so that future generations draw on the resource wealth and not only the current one.
rationales.C: The country discovered an extremely large deposit of crucial rare earth metals and formed the sovereign wealth fund in order to grow that capital for future generations. That is what defines a savings fund: it shares wealth across generations by transforming non-renewable assets, which deplete as they are extracted and sold, into a diversified portfolio of financial assets, which does not. The horizon is multi-generational rather than annual, which is why such a fund can carry a large allocation to equities and to illiquid alternatives.

questions.stem: A $50 billion sovereign wealth savings fund with a long-term investment horizon holds real estate at 15% of total assets, infrastructure at 10%, private capital at 10%, hedge funds at 10%, and natural resources at 5%, with the balance of the portfolio in equities, fixed income, and cash. The fund's total allocation to alternative investments is closest to:

rationales.A: The alternatives sleeve is half the fund, not nearly all of it. Real estate 15%, infrastructure 10%, private capital 10%, hedge funds 10%, and natural resources 5% sum to 50% of the $50 billion portfolio. A 90% figure would leave no room for the equities 40%, fixed income 9%, and cash 1% that make up the rest of the total portfolio.
rationales.B: 10% would be a small satellite sleeve. Infrastructure alone is 10% of total assets, so the alternatives total cannot also be 10%: adding real estate 15%, private capital 10%, hedge funds 10%, and natural resources 5% brings the total to 50% of the $50 billion fund.
rationales.C: Approximately 50% of assets are invested in alternative investments, consistent with the fund's long-term objectives. The split within alternatives is real estate 15%, infrastructure 10%, private capital 10%, hedge funds 10%, and natural resources 5%, and the total portfolio is therefore alternatives 50%, equities 40%, fixed income 9%, and cash 1%. A savings fund with no liability-driven cash flow needs and a multi-generational horizon can bear an illiquidity allocation of that size, which is the point of the long-term orientation.

questions.stem: A $50 billion sovereign wealth savings fund that makes no regular liability payments takes two direct investments whose exit timing it controls: $100 million of equity in an airport concession, which is 0.2% of total assets, and $25 million for a minority stake in a private company, which is 0.05% of total assets. Liquidity risk is most likely to be identified as significant for:

options.A: both investments.
options.B: neither investment.
options.C: the private stake only.

rationales.A: Liquidity risk is the main risk long-term institutional investors face, particularly during a significant market decline, so it is the natural first answer for two illiquid direct holdings. It does not apply at this scale. The positions are 0.2% and 0.05% of total assets, the fund has no cash flow pressure from the regular payment of liabilities, and direct ownership gives it control and discretion over when to exit.
rationales.B: Liquidity risk is not expected to be flagged as significant for either investment. Each represents a small portion of the fund's total assets, 0.2% and 0.05%, so neither forces a sale. The fund has no cash flow pressure, unlike institutional investors that face the regular payment of liabilities, and it has been growing over time while making a concerted effort to expand its direct investment program. Direct investments also mitigate some of the liquidity issues commonly experienced when investing through a fund, because direct ownership provides a greater amount of control and discretion over when to exit.
rationales.C: The reasoning that clears the airport concession clears the private stake as well: small position size, no cash flow pressure, and control over exit timing. The conclusion rests on those three features and not on a distinction driven by the concession's ongoing operating cash flows, so there is nothing to separate the two holdings on liquidity. The private stake is in fact the smaller of them, at 0.05% of assets against the concession's 0.2%.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund takes a stake in a greenfield airport built under a build-operate-transfer concession, alongside an airport operator that will run the terminal for a fee. The financing of the project most likely consists of:

options.A: equity from the fund alone.
options.B: non-recourse project debt plus sponsor equity.
options.C: sponsor equity with no debt.

rationales.A: The fund is one of several providers of capital rather than the only one. It contributes $100 million of a $500 million project cost, about 0.2% of its assets; the airport operator contributes $33 million and takes a fixed fee plus or minus a performance incentive; and lenders provide $300 million. Funding the whole project alone would also concentrate construction and traffic risk that the concession structure is designed to share.
rationales.B: Total project cost is $500 million for a terminal sized at 5 million passengers. The fund puts in $100 million, 0.2% of its assets, the airport operator $33 million, and $300 million is non-recourse project finance debt, giving roughly a 70/30 debt-to-equity structure with a 15-year tenor following a 3-year grace period. The concession runs 25 years including the 2-year construction period, a 35% quarterly concession fee is paid to the airport authority on all revenue, and airport charges, about 70% of revenue, are regulated by the concession contract under an inflation-linked formula. Expected return over the full 25-year term is a 15% internal rate of return. Non-recourse debt is the standard build-operate-transfer arrangement: lenders look to project cash flows, so sponsor loss is capped at the equity contributed.
rationales.C: An all-equity structure would leave out the $300 million of non-recourse project financing, which is about 70% of the $500 million cost and is the leverage that lifts the expected equity return to 15%.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund's private equity team agrees a direct investment in a beverage company whose founder is keen to modernize the plant but is unwilling to give up control of the business. The investment most likely takes the form of:

options.A: full ownership of the company.
options.B: a controlling equity stake.
options.C: a significant minority stake.

rationales.A: The founder is willing to sell only 35% and retains the other 65%, so full ownership is not on offer at any price. The fund pays $25 million for that 35%, which is a small commitment for a fund with $50 billion of assets: 0.05% of total assets and about 0.4% of total private equity assets.
rationales.B: 35% is a significant minority, not control. The founder keeps 65% precisely because he is worried about giving up control, and that is the condition on which the deal is done. What the stake does buy is influence rather than control: the board expands from five members to seven, with the fund taking two seats, one of them for the head of private equity.
rationales.C: The founder is keen on modernizing the plant but worried about giving up control, so he is willing to sell only a minority stake of 35%, in exchange for $25 million, of which $20 million goes to plant modernization. For a fund with $50 billion of assets this is a small investment, 0.05% of total assets and about 0.4% of total private equity assets. With a significant minority the fund is allowed two seats on the board, which expands from five members to seven. The company has revenue of $50 million and EBITDA of $7 million, a 14% margin, priced at a 10 times EBITDA multiple.

questions.stem: A frontier market beverage company's competitive position rests on a tariff of up to 100% on imported beverages, and a national election is approaching. The key risk to the equity investment case is most likely:

options.A: no material risk from the tariff.
options.B: removal of the tariff after the election.
options.C: tightening of the tariff after the election.

rationales.A: The tariff is the central identified vulnerability in the case rather than a non-issue. The company's competitive advantage relies on tariffs as high as 100% on foreign beverages, and with an election coming up the head of risk asks directly whether those entry barriers could fall away.
rationales.B: The entry barrier can disappear after the election, and that is the risk raised. The company's competitive advantage relies on a tariff of as much as 100% on imported beverages; if the tariff is reduced and import markets open up, foreign majors with much deeper pockets can enter and wait out a price war the company cannot afford. The committee's response is to apply a probability to a tariff reduction and to the import market opening rather than to treat the protection as permanent, which is the appropriate way to price a policy-dependent moat in a frontier market.
rationales.C: The risk runs the other way. Tighter protection would reinforce the company's position and raise, not lower, the value of the stake; the concern is that the tariff wall falls after the election and dissolves the competitive advantage the valuation depends on.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund holds a concession on an airport in a country that is expressly seeking international tourism. Regulated airport charges are 70% of project revenue and commercial sources are the other 30%. Revenue-side currency risk is most likely mitigated because:

options.A: most of the revenue is priced in dollars.
options.B: the local currency is stable.
options.C: revenue is hedged with currency forwards.

rationales.A: Airport charges are 70% of revenue, and it is typical for collection of those regulated charges to be outsourced to international organizations such as IATA, which collect from the airlines and remit almost all of it in dollars. The remaining 30% of commercial revenue is earned in a locale expressly seeking international tourism, so pricing is geared to international markets and the operator has the freedom to price in dollars there as well. The revenue line is therefore mostly dollar denominated, which also matches the currency the project's debt service is paid in.
rationales.B: The mitigation comes from the currency the revenue is priced in, not from the behaviour of the local currency. A frontier market currency can move wildly against the dollar, which is precisely why the structure routes 70% of revenue through dollar-denominated regulated charges and prices the commercial 30% in dollars as well.
rationales.C: No rolling forward program is needed or used here, and hedging a frontier currency would be costly where it is possible at all. The mitigation is structural: dollar-denominated airport charges collected through international organizations such as IATA, and commercial revenue priced in dollars for international tourists.

questions.stem: An airport concession in a frontier market is funded in part with $300 million of long-term non-recourse project debt, a size and tenor that banks in that country do not yet have the capacity to provide. The project's debt-side currency exposure is most likely:

options.A: dollar denominated.
options.B: unhedged.
options.C: local currency denominated.

rationales.A: The lenders are large international banks. In-country banks may participate, but given the size of the loans and how long term these arrangements are, the local banks simply do not have the capacity yet. Those international lenders are comfortable knowing the investors earn their returns mostly in dollars, and the $300 million of debt is denominated in dollars accordingly, so debt service and project revenue sit in the same currency.
rationales.B: The exposure is naturally hedged rather than left open. About 70% of project revenue is regulated airport charges collected in dollars and the commercial remainder can be priced in dollars, so dollar debt service is met out of dollar receipts and no derivatives overlay is required.
rationales.C: Borrowing locally is the intuitive assumption, since it keeps the lenders happy and the logistics simple, but the in-country banks lack the capacity for loans of this size and tenor. The debt is raised from international banks and denominated in dollars, so the exposure is not in the local currency.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund makes a direct private equity investment in a frontier market where the US dollar is in wide local use and the local currency is costly, and in some cases impossible, to hedge. The fund's currency exposure on that investment is most likely:

options.A: hedged with long-dated forwards.
options.B: fully hedged.
options.C: left unhedged.

rationales.A: Long-dated forwards on a frontier currency are the least available tool of all: these currencies are hard and costly to hedge, and some cannot be hedged at any sensible price. No forward program is proposed for this investment. The private equity view is simply that the exposure is not a worry, because the investor and most other visitors to the country transact in dollars.
rationales.B: The exposure is not hedged. The stated comfort rests on the dollar being in wide local use, not on any hedge having been put in place, and a frontier currency is hard to hedge in the first place.
rationales.C: The head of private equity is not stressed about the currency, on the grounds that he and most other visitors to the country are using US dollars, so the exposure is carried unhedged. The head of risk flags the weakness in that reasoning: it is hard to hedge these currencies, and meanwhile they can move wildly against the dollar, turning a really good investment into a really bad one. Local dollar usage is not a hedge for a position whose value and exit proceeds are generated in the local economy. Three years later a currency devaluation does occur, which validates the risk concern.

questions.stem: A 25-year greenfield airport concession has a base case IRR of 15%. Construction is covered by a fixed-price contract whose language passes any penalties for delayed or subpar construction down to the contractor, and the sponsor also runs reasonable low and high traffic cases. The largest reduction in the project's IRR most likely comes from:

options.A: low traffic, with an IRR of 10% to 11%.
options.B: cost overruns, with an IRR of 13%.
options.C: a shorter concession term, with an IRR of about 5%.

rationales.A: Analysis of the reasonable low case puts the IRR down to around 10% or 11%, while the high case pushes the return out into the high teens. Traffic is the dominant sensitivity. Capital expenditure risk is managed through the fixed-price contract, which passes construction penalties to the contractor, and a 10% sensitivity applied around that cost does impinge on the IRR a little bit but not as much as the low-traffic case. Even real cost overruns or delays leave about a 13% IRR, against 10% to 11% for low traffic, so traffic volume is the variable that moves the return most.
rationales.B: Real cost overruns or delays leave the project at about a 13% IRR, a smaller fall from the 15% base case than the low-traffic case produces. The 10% sensitivity run around capital expenditure does impinge on the IRR a little bit but not as much as the low-traffic case, partly because the fixed-price contract passes penalties for delay and subpar construction down to the contractor. Traffic, not capital expenditure, is therefore the largest sensitivity.
rationales.C: The concession runs 25 years by its own terms, so its length is not one of the variables the sponsor flexes. The sensitivities that are run bracket the 15% base case with the traffic cases, around 10% to 11% on the low side and the high teens on the high side, and an IRR of roughly 5% sits well outside the range the project's own analysis produces.

questions.stem: For a sovereign wealth fund holding the equity in a 25-year build-operate-transfer airport concession, traffic risk is most likely the largest financial risk because:

options.A: construction cost overruns revert to the fund whenever traffic falls below projections.
options.B: airport charges are unregulated and reprice automatically with traffic.
options.C: the airport's cash flows depend on the actual number of visitors.

rationales.A: Construction cost risk is largely passed to the contractor through the fixed-price construction contract, and it does not revert to the equity holder when traffic disappoints. Traffic risk is the larger exposure for a different reason: visitor volumes drive the concession's cash flows directly, on both the regulated airport charges and the commercial revenue.
rationales.B: Airport charges under this type of concession are regulated concession charges rather than free-floating prices, so they do not reprice automatically with traffic and cannot amplify revenue swings that way. The exposure is instead that actual visitor numbers fall short of the projections underpinning both airport charges, which are about 70% of revenue, and commercial revenue.
rationales.C: The airport's cash flows depend on the actual number of visitors and tourists moving through the terminal relative to the projections used at underwriting. Lower traffic cuts airport charges, roughly 70% of revenue, and commercial revenue at the same time, while most of the cost base is fixed. Over a 25-year concession the volume exposure is wide: pandemic risk, which scientists warn is becoming more likely; a prolonged global recession, in which discretionary vacation spending collapses and which is severe for a small island economy dependent on tourism; and long-term climate risk such as sea-level rise and extreme heat. Any of these could substantially depress traffic and therefore revenue, and none of them is transferred to a counterparty the way construction cost risk is.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund holds the equity in an airport concession financed with non-recourse project debt that carries a built-in debt-service reserve. Against an interruption in traffic revenue, these two features most likely provide:

options.A: unlimited protection for as long as the interruption lasts.
options.B: no protection against a revenue interruption.
options.C: coverage for a limited period, after which the financing may need restructuring.

rationales.A: The protection is limited in time, not unlimited. The debt-service reserve is sized to cover debt service for a defined period; if traffic is halted for longer than that, restructuring, rescheduling or fresh rescue capital becomes necessary. No reserve of finite size can bridge an interruption of indefinite length.
rationales.B: The reserve exists precisely to bridge a temporary interruption in revenue, so protection is real rather than absent, and the non-recourse structure separately caps the equity holder's loss at the project. What is limited is the duration of the cover, not its existence.
rationales.C: The built-in debt-service reserve covers debt service for a period of time in the event of a temporary revenue disruption such as a pandemic. If travel is on hold for much longer than that period, the sponsor turns to restructuring or rescheduling the financing. The 2020 pandemic was a turning point here: the language and dynamics of certain contractual agreements were adjusted so that cases like it could be worked out rather than becoming straight defaults, and the concern is the short-term impact, whereas over a 25-year horizon conditions are expected to recover gradually. The non-recourse structure limits the fund's downside as an equity investor to the project's own cash flows, with no claim running back to the fund's other assets, so the two features together convert a solvency threat into a timing and renegotiation problem.

questions.stem: Three years after a sovereign wealth fund acquired a beverage producer in the frontier market of Atsui, the region is in recession, a currency devaluation is anticipated, a new government has cut tariffs on imported beverages from 100% to 20%, local law requires two years' notice to terminate an employee, and sales are slowing. The fund's financial risk picture for the holding most likely shows:

options.A: improvement across its operating conditions.
options.B: no change from the initial investment view.
options.C: deterioration on several fronts at once.

rationales.A: The three-year picture is a catalog of negatives rather than an improvement: Atsui and surrounding nations went into recession, a currency devaluation is anticipated, tariff protection on imported beverages has been cut from a 100% tariff to a 20% tariff, which erodes the local producer's cost advantage over foreign brands, and labor rules are restrictive. No operating condition moved in the company's favor.
rationales.B: Conditions deteriorated significantly on several fronts simultaneously, so the risk picture is no longer the one underwritten at entry. Treating it as unchanged would leave the recession, the anticipated devaluation, the loss of tariff protection and the rigid labor rules unpriced.
rationales.C: Several financial risks materialized together. The regional recession matters more than it would elsewhere because beverages are considered a luxury item in Atsui, so volumes are highly cyclical and sales are slowing. An anticipated currency devaluation reduces the value of local-currency cash flows and of the stake itself when translated for the fund. The tariff cut from 100% to 20% removes most of the protection that made domestic production cheaper than imported brands, compressing margins just as demand weakens. Strict labor law, under which terminating the employment of an Atsui citizen requires significant notice of two years, makes the cost base rigid at the moment flexibility is most valuable, and the recently increased direct investing capability and modern equipment reduce the headcount the plant actually needs. The result is simultaneous pressure on revenue, margin, translated value and cost flexibility.

questions.stem: To manage the risk that future borrowing rates on a long-dated airport project exceed the levels forecast at underwriting, the equity sponsor most appropriately:

options.A: hedges its interest rate exposure on the project.
options.B: relies on CPI-linked concession charges to offset rate increases.
options.C: shifts the project to floating-rate funding from local banks.

rationales.A: The sponsor can manage the risk that actual future borrowing interest rates will be higher than forecast by hedging the project's interest rate exposure, using interest rate swaps or similar instruments to fix or cap the cost of funds. Long-dated project debt is particularly sensitive to rate risk, because a small change in the borrowing rate compounds over a concession of 25 years and feeds straight into the equity cash flows that sit behind the debt service.
rationales.B: No inflation-linked charge formula is described as offsetting borrowing costs, and inflation linkage on revenue is in any case an imperfect and indirect hedge of nominal interest expense: real rates can rise without inflation doing so, and regulated concession charges reset on their own schedule rather than with the funding curve. The direct remedy is to hedge the interest rate exposure itself.
rationales.C: Floating-rate funding would increase, not manage, sensitivity to higher future borrowing rates, since every rate rise would pass immediately into debt service and into the project's coverage ratios. Managing the exposure means moving toward certainty of funding cost through a hedge, not toward greater rate pass-through.

questions.stem: Five years into a 25-year airport concession, revenue is running about 50% below the base case because tourist numbers are short of forecast, costs are about 50% above the base case because of mitigating flood damage, and the medium-term forecast is weak. Relative to the base case, the investment most likely shows:

options.A: no material change.
options.B: outperformance.
options.C: continued underperformance.

rationales.A: The deviation from the base case is substantial on both sides of the income statement at once, so the position is not materially unchanged: revenue is about 50% lower than base case while costs are about 50% higher.
rationales.B: The financial risks identified at underwriting materialized rather than failing to appear, which leaves the project behind the base case rather than ahead of it.
rationales.C: The infrastructure investment continues to perform poorly because of a combination of lower revenue against forecast, about 50% below base case on fewer tourists, and higher costs against forecast, about 50% above base case for mitigating flood damage, with a medium- and long-term forecast that does not look promising. Both drivers were flagged as risks at underwriting and both have now been validated: the traffic risk, where the concession's cash flows ride on actual visitor numbers against projection, and the physical climate risk of siting a runway less than a kilometer from a rising sea. Because the debt-service reserve and the non-recourse structure only bridge a temporary disruption, underperformance of this size and persistence points toward restructuring or rescheduling the financing rather than toward waiting for the base case to reassert itself.

drills.los_text: discuss environmental and social risks associated with the portfolio strategy of an institutional investor
drills.reading_name: Case Study in Portfolio Management: Institutional (SWF)

questions.stem: Physical climate risks to real assets most likely include:

options.A: carbon pricing and coal phase-out policies.
options.B: consumer boycotts of high-emitting companies.
options.C: rising sea levels flooding coastal properties.

rationales.A: Carbon pricing and coal phase-out policies are climate transition risks: they arise from the policy and technology response to warming, not from the weather itself. They erode the value of fossil-fuel exposed holdings, but they are not the physical risk channel the question asks about.
rationales.B: Boycott-driven reputational harm is a social and reputational risk. It can damage a portfolio company's revenue, but it is a consequence of stakeholder behavior rather than of a physical climate hazard acting on an asset.
rationales.C: Physical climate risk is damage or impairment done to the asset itself by the climate. Rising sea levels that lead to flooding would affect both rents and property valuation for hitherto prime coastal properties. Prolonged exposure to extreme heat would negatively affect the useful life of roads and train tracks, leading to accelerated depreciation of those assets and therefore more frequent replacement costs for the companies and governments that own them. Physical damage from frequent, large-scale weather-related events such as hurricanes or wildfires, once considered too irregular to insure against, can both cause large-scale drawdowns in the portfolio's asset value and make the assets difficult or expensive to insure at all. Most flooding-related losses around the world are uninsured, so the loss stays with the asset owner.

questions.stem: Climate transition risks most likely include:

options.A: no material investment exposures.
options.B: carbon pricing, technological displacement, and stranded assets.
options.C: the same exposures as physical climate risks.

rationales.A: Policy shifts, technological displacement and stranded assets are real and measurable investment exposures, so the transition is not risk-free. Treating it as such leaves a portfolio unhedged against repricing that is already underway.
rationales.B: Transition risk is the risk arising from the move to a low-carbon economy: policy responses such as carbon pricing, coal phase-outs and bans on internal combustion engine sales; technological displacement of incumbent business models; and assets stranded before the end of their economic lives. The driver is the 2015 Paris Agreement target of limiting the global temperature increase this century to 2 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, for which scientists project that energy-related carbon dioxide emissions need to fall 25% by 2030 and reach net zero by 2070. Delivering that implies carbon prices in the range of US$40 to US$80 per ton of carbon dioxide by 2030 for first movers, which changes the cash flows of emitting assets directly rather than through any weather event.
rationales.C: Transition risks and physical risks are distinct channels. Carbon pricing, coal phase-outs and engine bans act through policy and technology, whereas storms, floods and extreme heat act on the asset physically. The two can offset or compound each other and need to be assessed separately.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund is reviewing a 25-year concession to expand an airport on a low-lying island, where the new runway sits less than a kilometer from the sea. Over that horizon, the project's most significant physical climate risk is most likely:

options.A: extreme heat shortening the runway's useful life.
options.B: sea-level rise flooding the runway site.
options.C: aviation carbon pricing reducing flight volumes.

rationales.A: Prolonged exposure to extreme heat does shorten the useful life of surfaces such as roads and train tracks and accelerate their depreciation, so this is a genuine physical risk, but it is not the binding one here. For a runway sited less than a kilometer from a rising sea, the exposure that can stop operations outright is water, not surface wear.
rationales.B: Sea-level rise may be gradual, but it does not stop, and the new runway is less than a kilometer from the sea. Over a 25-year investment horizon that is long enough for the risk to materialize and impair operations: the risk of flooding could become real even just during high tide, and running an airport in those conditions would not be possible. Weather is also becoming more erratic year over year, and climate risk and extreme weather have featured among the top risks in the World Economic Forum's Global Risks Report every year since 2017. The concession therefore pairs a long fixed horizon with an asset whose single most valuable component is at the waterline, which is why flooding dominates the physical risk assessment even where drainage has been engineered for once-in-50-years and once-in-100-years scenarios.
rationales.C: Carbon pricing on aviation is a climate transition risk, driven by policy rather than by a physical hazard acting on the asset. It could affect flight volumes and therefore traffic, but it is not the physical climate risk the question asks about.

questions.stem: An infrastructure team dismisses climate risk on a 25-year coastal airport concession, citing expert advice that environmental risks are unlikely to materialize within the horizon and drainage engineered for once-in-50-years and once-in-100-years flood scenarios. Three years later, seas have risen and storms are more frequent. That dismissal is most likely:

options.A: validated by subsequent events.
options.B: reasonable at the time but overtaken by events.
options.C: irrelevant to the project's risk governance.

rationales.A: Events do not validate the dismissal; they undercut it. Within three years, climate change had led to rising seas and more frequent storms, storms being common in island nations but the rising seas being the new concern, and hotter temperatures added a further concern. By year five, the cost of mitigating flood damage was running about 50% above the base case.
rationales.B: The dismissal rested on two supports that looked sound when it was made: expert advice that, in the time frame being considered, environmental risks were unlikely to materialize, and engineered mitigation during design, where drainage systems were modified to handle increases in groundwater levels and the engineers built in once-in-50-years and once-in-100-years flood scenarios that they were confident they could build for. Both supports proved insufficient. By the three-year update, climate change had produced rising seas, more frequent storms and hotter temperatures, and by year five the project was carrying costs about 50% above base case specifically to mitigate flood damage. The flaw is structural rather than careless: a design standard calibrated to a stationary distribution of flood events, and expert comfort anchored to a shorter time frame, were applied to an exposure that keeps growing across a 25-year concession, so the initial comfort was misplaced.
rationales.C: The dismissal is central to the project's risk governance rather than irrelevant to it: accepting expert assurance and an engineering design standard as a substitute for monitoring and repricing a long-dated physical risk is exactly the failure the subsequent updates expose.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund owns a beverage producer in the frontier market of Atsui. With the region in recession and sales slowing, the plant may need to cut factory jobs, and local law requires two years' notice to terminate an employee. The risks this raises for the fund are most likely:

options.A: environmental only, with no social dimension.
options.B: financial only, with no social concerns.
options.C: social, including reputational and community impact.

rationales.A: Firing factory workers in a frontier market during a recession, where terminating the employment of a citizen requires significant notice of two years, is a social and reputational exposure in its own right, so the risk set is not exclusively environmental even where environmental issues are also present.
rationales.B: Workforce and community issues are prominent here, so the exposure is not purely financial. The cost of the two-year notice period is a financial consequence of a social constraint, and the publicity risk attaches to the fund's standing as a state investor rather than to the holding's cash flows.
rationales.C: For a sovereign wealth fund there is direct reputational risk: flying in from world cities and firing factory employees in a frontier market means bad publicity, especially in Atsui and especially during a recession. Labor laws in Atsui are strict, and terminating the employment of an Atsui citizen requires significant notice of two years, which raises both the cost and the visibility of any workforce reduction just as increased direct investing capability and modern equipment reduce the headcount the plant needs. Because the owner is an arm of the state, the exposure runs to the government itself, with a headline such as government of Ruritania cuts jobs in XYZ during a recession illustrating the damage. In a small frontier economy the plant is also a significant local employer, so the community impact of job cuts is material alongside the fund's own reputation.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund's directly held beverage plant has cut costs by no longer paying to transport its non-toxic waste off site for proper treatment. The environmental risk this creates most likely involves:

options.A: Dumping the waste into a nearby river.
options.B: Contaminating groundwater with toxic chemicals.
options.C: Creating no environmental impact at all.

rationales.A: Plant management, trying to make up for lower profits, began dumping the waste into the nearby river rather than transporting it for proper treatment. Although the waste is not toxic, it is starting to spoil the lovely fishing spot near the factory, and scientists say the plant site and the river overlap with the range of a rare reptile found here and in only one other place on earth. A local endangered species issue of this kind draws attention from people with no interest in soda or mangoes, so the harm runs beyond the river itself to the fund's standing as an owner.
rationales.B: The waste being disposed of is not toxic, and the damage runs through surface water rather than groundwater: dumping into the river spoiled a local fishing spot and intruded on the habitat of a rare reptile. Toxic chemical contamination of groundwater is a different exposure and is not the one this cost-cutting created.
rationales.C: Real damage occurred to a community resource. The fishing spot near the factory is being spoiled, and the dumping reaches the range of a rare reptile found in only one other place on earth, so treating the saving as environmentally neutral understates both the environmental harm and the reputational exposure the fund now carries.

questions.stem: A plant held as a direct investment by a sovereign wealth fund is cutting operating costs. A social, rather than environmental, risk arising from that cost-cutting is most likely:

options.A: Raising local factory wages.
options.B: Discharging untreated waste into the river.
options.C: Shortening employee rest breaks.

rationales.A: Raising wages to retain skilled workers adds cost, while the risk in question arises from taking cost out. A pay rise is an employee-welfare benefit running in the opposite direction of the plant's cost-cutting, so it is not a social risk created by it.
rationales.B: River dumping is an environmental risk rather than one of the social risks the question targets. It belongs with waste handling and habitat damage, not with the treatment of the workforce.
rationales.C: The plant's cost-cutting reached employee breaks, reduced from one hour to 30 minutes, and the restrooms, where soap was removed and employees were asked to bring their own. As the fund's own discussion puts it: 'I know we're a $56 billion sovereign wealth fund, and here we are talking about removing soap from a few bathrooms in the tropics where we have a $25 million direct investment, but stuff like this can have a reputational impact.' Small-dollar decisions about working conditions can have outsized reputational effects, which is why they register as social risk at the fund level and not merely as plant housekeeping.

questions.stem: For large apparel brands and branded technology hardware companies, the supply chain risk of greatest ESG concern most likely involves:

options.A: Environmental emissions in logistics.
options.B: Labor management lapses at suppliers.
options.C: Lapses borne only by contract manufacturers.

rationales.A: The supply chain concern for these brands is labor management, not logistics emissions. Labor lapses carry both reputational damage and direct financial cost through consumer boycotts, product recalls and fines, which is what makes them the dominant supply chain exposure here.
rationales.B: Large brands in the apparel industry, such as Nike and Gap, and in the technology space, such as Apple and Samsung, have all been accused of various levels of lapses in their supply chain related to labor management issues. Apart from suffering significant damage to their brands and reputations, which could lead to consumer boycotts, such companies may also face additional costs and fines related to product recalls and the ad hoc shifting of supply chains.
rationales.C: The brand owners themselves, Nike, Gap, Apple and Samsung among them, absorbed the accusations and the reputational damage, along with recall costs and the cost of rearranging supply. The risk does not stay with the contract manufacturers where the labor practices occur; it travels up to the brand and therefore to the brand's shareholders.

questions.stem: For a sovereign wealth fund with equity exposure to the largest apparel brands and branded technology hardware companies, supply chain ESG issues are most likely:

options.A: Of paramount importance.
options.B: Of minimal importance.
options.C: Of importance only to retailers.

rationales.A: Considering such issues when making investments is of paramount importance, because a lack of transparency in the supply chain and lapses in labor management may weigh heavily on the resilience of those supply chains amid global-scale disruptions such as that caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. In addition to the financial risks, reputational risks may also arise from a view that the fund implicitly supports improper and unethical business practices.
rationales.B: For these exposures the issues are of paramount importance rather than peripheral. Opacity in supplier networks and labor management failures bear directly on supply chain resilience when global disruptions hit, and they expose the fund to the charge that it implicitly supports unethical practices.
rationales.C: Brand owners carry the reputational and resilience risk, not only the retailers who sell the goods. Opacity and labor lapses in supplier networks weigh on the equity value of the brands themselves, so a shareholder such as the fund is exposed through its holdings and through the perception that it condones those practices.

questions.stem: The just transition concept is most likely:

options.A: Permission to ignore impacts on workers and communities.
options.B: A mandate to put environmental outcomes above people.
options.C: A mandate to limit social harm while pursuing environmental gains.

rationales.A: Attending to those impacts is the concept's entire content. The transition to environmentally sustainable economies displaces workers and costs jobs in industries such as coal mining, fossil fuel extraction and production, and fossil fuel-based power generation, and higher energy and commodity costs fall on poor households; a just transition exists precisely to keep those effects in view rather than to license ignoring them.
rationales.B: The concept balances the two rather than ranking one above the other: it limits negative social impacts while positive environmental impacts are pursued. Sustainable development means meeting the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, and a transition that impoverishes workers and poor households fails that test even if its environmental outcome is good.
rationales.C: In the transition to environmentally sustainable economies and societies, several challenges may arise, for example the displacement of workers and job losses in industries such as coal mining, fossil fuel extraction and production, and fossil fuel-based power generation. Similarly, increased energy costs due to carbon taxes, and higher commodity costs partly resulting from sustainable production practices, may have adverse effects on the incomes of poor households. A 'just' transition is therefore necessary to ensure that there are limited negative social impacts in the pursuit of positive environmental impacts, such as avoiding fossil fuels and adopting sustainable agriculture and business practices.

questions.stem: Climate mitigation opportunities most likely include investment in:

options.A: Clean energy, storage, smart grids, and transition materials.
options.B: Sustainable agriculture and flood-resilient infrastructure.
options.C: Natural gas combined-cycle generation.

rationales.A: Mitigation opportunities are companies positioned to benefit from efforts to curb long-term climate change: clean energy, covering wind, solar and small hydro generation as well as the manufacturers of windmills and solar panels; energy efficiency, covering energy-efficient transportation and building solutions and recycling; batteries and storage, where improved battery capacity and efficiency is the driver; smart grids, meaning digitally enhanced electricity grids; and materials such as copper and battery-grade lithium, key ingredients in the clean energy value chain.
rationales.B: Sustainable agriculture and flood-resilient infrastructure are climate adaptation examples. They help an economy adjust to climate change that occurs and reduce vulnerability to its harmful effects, rather than curbing the change itself, which is what mitigation investment does.
rationales.C: The mitigation opportunity set centres on clean energy, energy efficiency, batteries and storage, smart grids and transition materials, not on gas-fired generation. Gas combined cycle remains a fossil fuel technology, so it is not the long-term asset through which an investor expresses a mitigation view, even though its levelized cost sits below coal.

questions.stem: Climate adaptation opportunities most likely include:

options.A: Companies that reduce vulnerability to a changing climate.
options.B: Smart grid and battery-grade lithium companies.
options.C: Wind, solar, and battery storage companies.

rationales.A: The adaptation category includes companies that would help better adjust to actual or expected future change in climate with an aim to reduce vulnerability to the harmful effects of climate change, such as food insecurity, sea-level rise and frequent extreme weather events. Sustainable agriculture is the leading example: companies in that segment provide products that improve agricultural productivity and reduce resource use.
rationales.B: Smart grids and battery-grade lithium belong to the mitigation opportunity set, where investment curbs long-term climate change through digitally enhanced grids and the materials feeding the clean energy value chain. They are not businesses whose purpose is reducing vulnerability to climate change that has already occurred.
rationales.C: Wind, solar and battery storage are climate mitigation examples, aimed at curbing the extent of warming. Adaptation opportunities instead reduce vulnerability to the warming that occurs, as sustainable agriculture does by lifting productivity and cutting resource use in the face of food insecurity and extreme weather.

questions.stem: For banks, asset managers, and asset owners estimating how their businesses might perform under different degrees of global warming, the approach recommended by the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) is most likely:

options.A: Scenario analysis across several warming scenarios.
options.B: Single-point climate forecasts in place of scenarios.
options.C: No scenario analysis, as too speculative to disclose.

rationales.A: Given the uncertainty around the precise timing and magnitude of the impact of climate change, organizations are increasingly using climate-related scenario analysis to better understand how their businesses might perform under a variety of global warming scenarios, for example in a world that is 2°C, 3°C or 4°C warmer. The TCFD recommends that organizations, including banks, asset managers and asset owners, use scenario analysis to estimate the implications of such risks and opportunities for their businesses over time and also to inform their strategic thinking. The International Energy Agency and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change both publicly offer sets of climate-related scenarios that are widely used.
rationales.B: Multiple scenarios, not single-point forecasts, are what the TCFD recommends. The timing and magnitude of climate impacts are uncertain, so a single central projection hides exactly the range of outcomes, from a 2°C to a 4°C warmer world, that the analysis is meant to expose.
rationales.C: Scenario analysis is the TCFD's central recommended tool rather than something to be avoided, and ready-made scenarios from the International Energy Agency and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change are widely used for the purpose. Uncertainty about timing and magnitude is the reason for the technique, not a reason to omit it from disclosure.

questions.stem: Unsubsidized levelized costs of energy are estimated at $28-$54 per MWh for wind, $32-$42 for thin-film utility-scale solar PV, $44-$68 for gas combined cycle, $66-$152 for coal, and $118-$192 for nuclear. These estimates most likely indicate that:

options.A: generation technologies differ little in cost.
options.B: wind and utility-scale solar compete with coal on cost.
options.C: renewables cost more than conventional generation.

rationales.A: The differences are material, not negligible: the wind range of $28-$54 per MWh and the thin-film utility-scale solar range of $32-$42 sit below the gas combined cycle range of $44-$68, well below coal at $66-$152, and far below nuclear at $118-$192. The top of the coal range is more than five times the bottom of the wind range, so cost ranking is precisely what these figures establish.
rationales.B: Wind at $28-$54 per MWh and thin-film utility-scale solar PV at $32-$42 undercut coal at $66-$152 and overlap the lower end of gas combined cycle at $44-$68, all on an unsubsidized basis. This cost competitiveness, coupled with the urgency to decarbonize economies to avoid the potentially catastrophic physical impacts of climate change, has created a secular growth opportunity for such businesses and assets, thereby attracting increasingly large investor attention.
rationales.C: The figures show the opposite for wind and utility-scale solar, which come in below both coal and nuclear and reach into the gas combined cycle range without subsidy. A claim that renewables remain the expensive option misses the shift in relative costs that underpins the investment case for clean energy.

questions.stem: For a fund holding a direct investment in a local operating business, a social license to operate most likely means:

options.A: Regulatory approval alone.
options.B: A government permit covering labor practices.
options.C: Community relations as a condition of operating.

rationales.A: A social license is broader than regulatory compliance. Permits and approvals satisfy the authorities, but the fund's ability to keep operating also depends on the acceptance of the people living around the plant, which no regulator grants and no approval secures.
rationales.B: A social license is not a legal document or a government permit. It is the community's ongoing acceptance of the investor's operations, earned through community relations and engagement, and it can be withdrawn by that community even while every formal permit remains in force.
rationales.C: Community relations is a key component of the ability to operate. The fund plans new community programs around the restructuring, aiming to make a positive impact first: cutting employees is sensitive, so by helping many more people than it lets go and giving employees proper training so they have the skills for whatever they do next, it intends to be part of a sensible transition. Transparent handling of environmental impacts such as the waste dumping, and lobbying for constructive solutions, work the same way. The framing bakes ESG into ongoing operational strategy rather than treating it as a compliance exercise.

drills.los_text: analyze and evaluate the financial and non-financial risk exposures in the portfolio strategy of an institutional investor
drills.reading_name: Case Study in Portfolio Management: Institutional (SWF)

questions.stem: For a sovereign wealth fund that invests for the long term in frontier markets and holds non-traded direct stakes, the risk exposure that is least likely to be relevant is:

options.A: Frontier-market currency risk.
options.B: Day-trading risk in commodities.
options.C: Long-horizon climate and environmental risk.

rationales.A: Market and currency risk is one of the fund's central exposures, and it is most acute in the frontier markets where its direct holdings sit, so this exposure is relevant rather than excluded.
rationales.B: The fund is a long-term investor holding non-tradable direct investments, not a day-trading commodity operation, so intraday commodity trading risk does not describe its exposures. The exposures that are relevant are: (1) market and currency risk, especially in frontier markets such as Sunnyland and Atsui; (2) climate and environmental risk on long-horizon infrastructure, including sea-level rise and extreme heat; (3) political and reputational risk around labor practices and pollution at the ABC holding; (4) macroeconomic and traffic risk, such as a pandemic or a recession; and (5) interest rate risk on project debt.
rationales.C: Climate and environmental risk is directly relevant: the infrastructure assets are held over horizons of 25 years or more, which exposes them to sea-level rise, more frequent storms and extreme heat.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund reviews a small direct holding whose plant may lay off workers in a recession and has been discharging waste into a local river; in that review, reputational risk is most likely:

options.A: Fully measurable in dollar terms.
options.B: The foremost concern.
options.C: Secondary to financial metrics.

rationales.A: The concern is qualitative and broad rather than a quantity to be priced: headlines about firing people during a recession, polluting the river, threatening endangered species and being petty about small staff amenities do not reduce to a dollar figure.
rationales.B: Reputational risk is treated as the biggest concern at the three-year review. The head of risk puts it as not wanting 'to end up in the newspaper firing people during a recession, polluting the river, threatening endangered species, and being rather petty about soap', and on that basis proposes exiting the investment as soon as possible; the head of infrastructure agrees on all counts. The chief investment officer adds that 'a small investment can have an outsized negative impact on us if we don't manage the risk properly'. Reputation is thereby elevated to the central concern of the review rather than one input among many.
rationales.C: Reputation is elevated above the financial metrics here, not subordinated to them: it is the consideration that drives the proposal to exit a holding that is only a fraction of a percent of assets.

questions.stem: For a sovereign wealth fund, a direct private equity stake amounting to a very small share of total assets most likely:

options.A: Carries reputational risk only if the stake is controlling.
options.B: Warrants monitoring in proportion to its portfolio weight.
options.C: Has an outsized reputational impact if poorly managed.

rationales.A: Headline risk attaches to the sovereign fund's involvement itself, whether or not the stake is controlling: a minority holder still appears in a headline such as 'Government of Ruritania Cuts Jobs in XYZ during a Recession'.
rationales.B: Materiality is not proportional to portfolio weight. The $25 million ABC stake is roughly 0.05% of assets, yet the chief investment officer stresses that 'even a small investment can have an outsized negative impact on us if we don't manage the risk properly', so it receives full investment committee attention rather than review delegated below committee level.
rationales.C: Despite representing about 0.05% of assets, the $25 million ABC stake draws scrutiny because of the fund's sovereign status: 'This is a rather small investment, of $25 million, but even a small investment can have an outsized negative impact on us if we don't manage the risk properly.' The headline risk, 'Government of Ruritania Cuts Jobs in XYZ during a Recession', is what makes the exposure large relative to the capital at stake, and it is larger for a sovereign owner than for a conventional private equity house.

questions.stem: On headline risk from job cuts at a portfolio company, the statement that best describes sovereign wealth funds relative to conventional private equity firms is that:

options.A: Conventional firms can more easily cut jobs for financial reasons.
options.B: The two types of investor face identical constraints.
options.C: Sovereign funds face no reputational constraints.

rationales.A: A conventional private equity house can cut jobs for purely financial reasons with less external constraint. For a sovereign wealth fund it is more complicated, because the government's name stands behind the investment: the chief investment officer asks the committee to imagine the headline 'Government of Ruritania Cuts Jobs in XYZ during a Recession', and the head of infrastructure answers that 'it's not a good look'. Sovereign status amplifies headline risk and narrows the set of acceptable actions at the portfolio company.
rationales.B: The constraints differ substantially: sovereign ownership attaches the government's name to every action taken at the portfolio company, which a conventional private equity owner does not face.
rationales.C: Sovereign status elevates reputational constraints rather than removing them, since the fund's actions are read as the government's actions; that is exactly why the job-cut headline is the committee's concern.

questions.stem: For long-horizon infrastructure underwritten on engineering assurances and 50-year and 100-year flood scenarios, the exposure most likely understated at inception and critical later is:

options.A: Commodity price risk.
options.B: Climate and environmental risk.
options.C: Operational risk.

rationales.A: Commodity prices are not the exposure that emerged; the deterioration came through the physical environment and the cost of protecting the asset against it.
rationales.B: Climate and environmental risk was dismissed at inception, when the head of infrastructure reported that experts said environmental risks were unlikely to materialize, resting on engineering assurances and 50-year and 100-year flood scenarios. Three years in, rising seas and more frequent storms were already affecting operations. By year five, the cost of mitigating flood damage was running 50% above the base case forecast. The head of equities' initial concern was validated by events, which is the general lesson: a risk whose horizon is longer than the underwriting scenario is the one most likely to be understated.
rationales.C: Operational problems did appear, but they were consequences of the environmental exposure: flooding and storm damage drove the mitigation spending, so naming operational risk alone misses the source of the loss.

questions.stem: For a fund whose listed equity positions can be sold within the hour, the contrast with its direct private holdings most likely highlights:

options.A: The difficulty of exiting direct private investments.
options.B: The equivalence of exit costs across the two.
options.C: The absence of any need to exit direct holdings.

rationales.A: A long horizon does not make an exit easier when the time comes, whether the decision is the fund's own or forced by outside pressure. The contrast drawn is with the head of equities, who was unhappy about how much one of his portfolio companies was polluting, simply sold the position, and was done within the hour because it was a liquid investment in a public market. Direct and private holdings offer no such route out, so reputational and operational problems there have to be managed rather than sold away.
rationales.B: Exit cost and exit speed differ enormously: a listed position can be closed within the hour, while a direct stake requires finding a buyer and negotiating terms over months or years.
rationales.C: The chief investment officer says the opposite, that 'our rather long-term horizon doesn't make it any easier for us to step away from an investment when the time comes'. Exits do occur, by the fund's own choice or under outside pressure; the long horizon makes them harder, not unnecessary.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund holds a minority stake, with two board seats, in a plant facing layoffs and pollution claims; its most appropriate response is most likely to:

options.A: Write the position down and wait out the holding period.
options.B: Exit at once, since a minority holder has no influence.
options.C: Engage management on remediation before considering exit.

rationales.A: The response proposed is active rather than passive: hand the holding to the distressed-asset team before it becomes properly distressed, engage management on how the business functions, and plan the workforce transition. Writing the position down and waiting changes none of the conduct that creates the reputational exposure.
rationales.B: Exit is one option among several, and remediation comes first; with two board seats the fund has direct channels for influencing the company's behavior, so a minority position does not leave it powerless.
rationales.C: The head of private equity proposes trying to salvage the investment before exiting it: pass ABC to the distressed-asset team 'before it becomes properly distressed', then ask whether the way the business functions can be changed to manage the risk. Management would be motivated to keep people inside and outside the plant happy and to shift to a less profit-driven focus, while further modernization capital makes less sense now. Workers facing redundancy would be paid about half their regular salary for eight months, with good training and assistance in finding another job. Alongside this, the fund would lobby the government for flexibility on labor law and stop the plant's dumping of waste.

questions.stem: With rigid host-country labor laws blocking a 50% workforce cut, and the company unlikely to survive if tariff protection falls to 20%, the fund's most effective approach to that government is most likely:

options.A: No approach, since the labor laws are rigid.
options.B: The argument that blocking partial cuts risks all the jobs.
options.C: A financial threat against the government.

rationales.A: Lobbying is a live option rather than a closed door, and the rigidity of the rules is the opening: legal roadblocks to cutting 50% of the jobs may put 100% of them at risk, because the company will not survive if tariffs are reduced to 20%.
rationales.B: The head of equities frames the pitch this way: if there are legal roadblocks to cutting 50% of the jobs, the government 'might be putting 100% of the jobs at risk because the company won't survive if tariffs are reduced to 20%'. The government does not want the factory to shut down because of its own rigid labor laws, so there is room for a negotiated conclusion that preserves part of the workforce instead of losing all of it. The leverage is the government's own objective, not the fund's capital.
rationales.C: The approach is reasoned framing of the government's own interest in keeping the factory open, not a threat. A sovereign investor threatening a host government would create precisely the diplomatic and reputational damage the fund is trying to avoid.

questions.stem: A rumor that the operator of a fund's airport concession wants to renegotiate its contract is most likely a risk the fund should:

options.A: Ignore as immaterial.
options.B: Address collaboratively with the operator.
options.C: Escalate directly to arbitration.

rationales.A: An operator's dissatisfaction is a genuine operational risk: if it activates a break clause in two or three years, the fund is left with the responsibility it least wants, which is finding a new operator for the asset.
rationales.B: The concession agreement is well structured and affords decent protection against meddling in the fee structure, with break clauses if matters get too far out of line and incentives that reward both sides when traffic rises. Even so, as the head of infrastructure puts it, 'we don't want a disgruntled operator. Happy employees, happy travelers, better experience, more traffic.' AOG is a strong global operator, and a break clause activated in two or three years' time would leave the fund responsible for replacing it. Cooperation remains satisfactory, so the recommendation is to see how the talks over the delays play out and to keep working with the operator.
rationales.C: Arbitration is premature while the operator's cooperation is still satisfactory. The collaborative posture protects traffic and the passenger experience, both of which a disgruntled operator would damage, and it preserves the incentive structure already written into the concession.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund seeks to exit a 35% stake in a loss-making beverage plant in a country where a weak local currency has hurt foreign exporters' sales; the stake is most likely to be:

options.A: Written off.
options.B: Sold to an international beverage company.
options.C: Liquidated at a total loss.

rationales.A: The stake was sold rather than written off: a buyer was found for the full 35% position at $27 million, against the fund's $25 million investment, so no write-down to zero was required.
rationales.B: The private equity team avoided a diplomatic crisis and reputational damage by finding a buyer for the full 35% stake and selling the whole position at $27 million. The buyer was an international beverage company that had been exporting into the country and whose sales had been hurt as the local currency weakened; producing locally is advantageous to that buyer because it provides a natural foreign exchange hedge. That is why the plant was worth more to the strategic buyer than to the fund, and why a trade sale was available even though the holding had become a problem asset.
rationales.C: The position was not a total loss: the full stake realized $27 million on a $25 million investment, and the sale also removed the fund's reputational and diplomatic exposure to the plant's labor and pollution problems.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund's three-year interim review reports that it is still ahead of its overall benchmark, though its margin of outperformance has been dulled by weak commercial real estate. Over those three years its assets under management most likely:

options.A: remained flat.
options.B: declined.
options.C: grew.

rationales.A: Assets under management did not hold at their starting level. At the three-year review the fund reported growth of $6 billion, from $50 billion to $56 billion, so a flat asset base is inconsistent with the update given.
rationales.B: Assets under management rose rather than fell. The three-year update records $6 billion of growth, to $56 billion, with the fund still ahead of its overall benchmark; what deteriorated was the margin of outperformance, not the size of the fund.
rationales.C: Assets under management grew by $6 billion over the three years, from $50 billion to $56 billion. The three-year update: 'In those three years, AUM have grown by $6 billion. We're still outperforming our overall benchmark, but our outperformance has been dulled by difficulties with some assets, primarily real estate, because commercial real estate has underperformed. So that's hurt us a little bit, but as ever, we are long-term investors.' Growth therefore came alongside narrower, not reversed, relative performance, with commercial real estate the identified drag.

questions.stem: R-SWF's assessment of political risk in Sunnyland is most likely:

options.A: low, given fair treatment of foreign investors and good government relations.
options.B: absent, since island nations carry no political risk.
options.C: low, given the stability of an authoritarian government.

rationales.A: The low rating rested on a track record of reasonable treatment of foreign investment, good government-to-government relations, and the island's geography. The head of private equity: 'Investment in Sunnyland has mostly been on the tourism side. There's a mixture of three- and five-star hotels, so major international hotel operators are around. And they're still arriving, but they feel the transportation bottleneck. Those who are there and the ones who are thinking about coming in are happy about the airport project.' The head of infrastructure: 'I haven't heard any horror stories about investors in Sunnyland getting burned because of unfair rule changes. Plus, relations are good. The Sunnyland authorities approached us as a fellow government institution.' The CIO: 'One nice thing about an island nation is that it is an island. There's less political interference from the neighbours.' Being approached as a fellow government institution matters as well, since it aligns the sponsor's interest with the investor's.
rationales.B: A political risk assessment was made, and reasoned. Earlier foreign investment in Sunnyland, concentrated in three- and five-star hotels with major international operators still arriving, had not been subject to unfair rule changes, and government-to-government relations were good. Island status was cited as one supporting factor, reducing political interference from neighbours, not as grounds for treating political risk as non-existent; no jurisdiction carries zero political risk, which is why the rating is low rather than absent.
rationales.C: The low rating rested on the treatment of past foreign investment, good government-to-government relations, R-SWF being approached as a fellow government institution, and the reduced scope for interference from neighbours that comes with being an island. The character of the regime is not the stated basis, and stability imposed by an authoritarian government would be a weak basis in any case, since the risk of abrupt, unilateral rule changes tends to be higher rather than lower in such settings.

questions.stem: R-SWF's initial dismissal of currency risk for ABC (Atsui) most likely proved to be:

options.A: correct.
options.B: irrelevant.
options.C: mistaken.

rationales.A: The initial view was not vindicated. The head of private equity's reasoning, 'I'm not stressed about it. When it comes to me and most other visitors to Atsui, we're using US dollars', spoke to the currency visitors spend rather than the currency in which ABC's earnings and eventual exit proceeds are denominated. A devaluation was anticipated by the three-year update, so the dismissal was overtaken by events.
rationales.B: Currency was central to the outcome, not peripheral to it. The head of risk warned that frontier market currencies 'can move wildly against the dollar, turning a really good investment into a really bad investment', and that exposure went on to bear directly on value: a devaluation was anticipated at the three-year update, and by the five-year point the buyer of the stake wanted local production as a natural hedge against the weaker currency.
rationales.C: The dismissal proved wrong, and the head of risk's concern about frontier market currencies moving 'wildly against the dollar, turning a really good investment into a really bad investment' was validated. The head of private equity had initially said, 'I'm not stressed about it. When it comes to me and most other visitors to Atsui, we're using US dollars.' At the three-year update, 'a currency devaluation is anticipated.' At five years, the buyer sought local production as a natural foreign exchange hedge against the weaker currency, confirming that the devaluation had occurred. Spending dollars as a visitor is not the same exposure as holding an asset whose cash flows are earned in local currency.

questions.stem: The R-SWF risk factor analysis framework most likely covers:

options.A: quantifiable market risks only.
options.B: equity, interest rate and credit risk only.
options.C: equity, interest rate, credit, inflation, currency and liquidity risk.

rationales.A: The framework is not confined to quantifiable market risk. The risk factor analysis combines quantitative modeling with qualitative assessment, and explicitly takes in qualitative exposures such as the potential reputational risk arising from certain types of investments, so excluding reputational risk as unquantifiable misstates the framework's reach.
rationales.B: Currency risk and liquidity risk sit inside the factor analysis itself, alongside equity, interest rate, credit and inflation risk. None of the six is handled outside the framework; the whole point of listing them together is that a single analysis maps the fund's exposures across all of them.
rationales.C: Institutional investors typically perform risk factor analysis to better understand the fund's risk exposures, such as exposure to equity risk, interest rate risk, credit risk, inflation risk, currency risk and liquidity risk. That analysis includes both quantitative modeling and qualitative risk assessments. The quantitative tools may involve sophisticated risk management systems based on returns or holdings, scenario analysis and stress testing. Other risks are more qualitative in nature, such as potential reputational risk from certain types of investments. The framework therefore spans six factor exposures and both modes of assessment.

questions.stem: R-SWF's risk mitigation actions over the course of the case study most likely include:

options.A: currency derivatives and put options on the ABC stake.
options.B: litigation against counterparties.
options.C: hedging, contract renegotiation, ESG engagement and a secondary sale.

rationales.A: The Atsui currency exposure was treated as hard or even impossible to hedge, and no put options on the ABC stake existed. Mitigation instead ran through interest rate hedging on the Sunnyland airport project, collaboration with AOG on delays and the concession extension, ESG engagement at ABC, and ultimately the sale of the stake.
rationales.B: Litigation barely features. The mitigation program was built on hedging the airport project's interest rate exposure, renegotiating and collaborating on the AOG contract, engaging on environmental and workforce issues at ABC, and selling the ABC stake; disputes were handled constructively rather than through the courts, which preserved the relationships the fund needed as a long-term investor.
rationales.C: R-SWF's risk management actions across the case include interest rate hedging for the Sunnyland airport project; constructive negotiation with AOG, including positive collaboration on delays and the concession extension; ESG engagement with ABC covering workforce transition and environmental cleanup; reframing ABC as an impact investment; the sale of the ABC stake for $27 million to an international beverage buyer; and proactive climate risk mitigation through drainage design, alongside ongoing reputational risk management. Risk management here is an ongoing process rather than a single action.

drills.los_text: discuss various methods to manage the risks that arise on long-term direct investments of an institutional investor
drills.reading_name: Case Study in Portfolio Management: Institutional (SWF)

questions.stem: For the Sunnyland airport, R-SWF's currency risk management is most likely based on:

options.A: extensive derivatives hedging.
options.B: structural alignment of US dollar revenues with US dollar debt.
options.C: matching local-currency debt against local-currency revenues.

rationales.A: No derivative hedging is described for the airport's currency exposure. The exposure is managed structurally instead, by arranging for revenues and debt to be denominated in the same currency, which removes the mismatch rather than offsetting it in the derivatives market.
rationales.B: The exposure is managed by structural currency alignment. On the revenue side, 70% of revenue is airport charges paid in US dollars through IATA, and the remaining 30% of commercial revenue is priced in US dollars because it targets international tourists. On the financing side, the $300 million of project debt is US dollar denominated. Revenue currency and debt currency therefore line up, and no derivative hedging is needed or described.
rationales.C: Both the $300 million of project debt and the revenue streams are US dollar denominated, so there is no local-currency debt set against local-currency revenue. The alignment is structural and it is in US dollars: 70% of revenue comes from airport charges paid in dollars through IATA, and the 30% commercial share is priced in dollars for international tourists.

questions.stem: R-SWF's exposure to borrowing rates higher than forecast on the Sunnyland airport project is most likely:

options.A: unavoidable, because the project debt is non-recourse.
options.B: manageable only by refinancing at maturity.
options.C: hedgeable with interest rate swaps.

rationales.A: The project financing structure does not prevent hedging. R-SWF can manage the risk that actual future borrowing rates turn out higher than forecast by hedging its interest rate exposure for the Sunnyland airport project, whatever the recourse characteristics of the debt; the exposure is economic and can be hedged on its own terms.
rationales.B: Waiting for maturity to refinance leaves the exposure unmanaged in the meantime, and exposes the project to whatever rates prevail on the refinancing date. The exposure can be hedged now, through interest rate swaps and similar instruments, which fixes the cost of funds over the period that matters.
rationales.C: R-SWF can manage the risk that actual future borrowing interest rates will be higher than forecast by hedging its interest rate exposure for the Sunnyland airport project. Interest rate risk on developed market borrowings is straightforward to hedge, through interest rate swaps and similar derivatives, which is precisely the contrast with the Atsui currency exposure: a frontier market currency is hard or impossible to hedge at acceptable cost, while an interest rate exposure of this kind is readily transferred.

questions.stem: For managing ABC's exposure to the consumer shift toward health foods, the most appropriate action is most likely to:

options.A: concentrate further on carbonated beverages.
options.B: exit the ABC position immediately.
options.C: develop healthy beverage alternatives.

rationales.A: Concentrating in the declining category is the risk itself rather than a response to it. The indicated path is to develop healthy alternatives, leveraging the experience gained producing the natural mango drink and extending into sports drinks and juices, so that the product mix moves with consumer preferences instead of against them.
rationales.B: Exit is premature. Product adaptation comes first: the company has demonstrated capability in healthier products and an expanding production facility to put behind them, so the value of the position can be defended operationally before any decision to sell is reached.
rationales.C: R-SWF can manage the risk of carbonated beverages falling out of favor, as preference for health foods increases, by working to develop new healthy alternatives to carbonated, presumably sugar-filled drinks. As the production facility expands its ability to produce product, ABC could focus its new product development on healthy alternatives.
